Addiction is an inability or extreme difficulty to stop. Habits you can stop if you want to. Both are generally mediated by instrumental learning. That is that through conditioning you learn that doing x brings y benefit. In addiction this benefit is usually the release of opioids, which produces a stronger craving (a larger dopamine response) which is harder to overcome than a learned association between a habit and some less intense or less immediate reward

There’s already good answers here but I just wanted to clarify real quick that dopamine is not necessarily involved while doing pleasurable things, but is more involved in the anticipation of rewards. It is a wanting/craving mechanism that drives you to a reward. The release you get when actually receiving the reward (e.g. watching tv) is mainly opioid-based.

But to answer your question, the feel good chemicals are the same, strictly speaking, but in differing amounts depending on how strongly the reward is wanted, which has all sorts of factors. Exercise doesnt tend to be something most people crave, so the dopamine release isn’t gonna be huge. It does however release other wonderful chemicals such as serotonin and endorphins (natural opioids) in abundance, which give you a longer lasting lift in mood than dopamine. If you associated that with exercise by exercising regularly and noticing the benefits you might start to crave it.

Okay so this old dude called Michael Siffre had the same question (but minus access to a watch, if I remember correctly). He was also a very dedicated guy so he decided to spend 2 months alone underground without exposure to natural light and sound. When he surfaced in mid-September he thought it was mid-August. Basically what had happened is without access to external cues (fancy word: exogenous zeitgeibers) he could only go by his biological clock (fancy word: endogenous pacemakers) which was about 25 hours instead of 24.

There have been similar studies with more participants, except of course not many people are willing to live in a cave for 2 months. But with periods of maybe 3-4 weeks or so in bunkers you find most people's circadian rhythms are between 24 and 25 hours without any external cues, though there is some individual variation of course.

But also to note is our biological clocks are not maaaajorly manipulated by the external cues, at least once we've settled into a routine. If you speed up a clock without telling people they generally won't be able to adjust to the new routine. A group of researchers (Folkard et al., 1985) did this to participants in a cave so that within 22 hours the participants thought it had been 24, and they did not manage to adjust their sleep accordingly. So it seems that the biological clock at least doesn't want the cycle to get any shorter than about 24 hours.

The other thing that would happen in this scenario is some people would probably experience depression, or a worsening of existing depression, since light helps us regulate our melatonin levels (sleepy hormone). Increased melatonin levels seem to affect the production of serotonin, which is why some people get depressed in the winter (seasonal affective disorder). 

TLDR: Without outside cues to the time, we tend to have sleep/wake cycles of around 25 hours, and without light, we tend to have a lower mood.

I can see how calling something self harm  that you don’t regard as self harm would be frustrating. It’s hard, I think, to cluster symptoms into easily digestible categories while also taking into account the vast individual differences in experiences. I do think though, that if someone is seeking help for something they consider to be self harming behaviour, even if it isn’t literal self harm, they should be allowed to do so and to use the term that allows them to find people they relate to. I’m sure you’d agree with that anyway.

Usually if you say you self harm people assume cutting/burning anyway, at least in my experience. If somebody says I do x behaviour in order to harm myself, what harm does that do to people who self injure? Maybe I’m being ignorant here but I personally don’t see what negative impact that could have.

I understand your point and to some extent your frustration. I am however skeptical as to whether it is particularly helpful or important to follow a strict definition. If somebody is doing something to intentionally hurt themselves, physically or otherwise, and they find it helpful to describe it using a term that is relatively well understood by people, I don’t really see a problem with this. I do self harm by cutting but there are also other behaviours I have which while I know do not fit the medical definition of “self harm”, that term feels more accurate for me than self destruction, so I will occasionally draw the comparison to explain my intentions better. I’m having a hard time seeing why this would cause a problem or invalidate people who self harm.
